lessons.title: How to actually learn a language
lessons.decision: What these lessons are, and what actually does the work

blocks.title: Why this comes first
blocks.text: If you skip this you'll use the rest of the course wrong. Two minutes here saves you months.

The reason adults fail at languages isn't that languages are hard. Children manage it, and they aren't smarter than you.

The reason is forgetting. You learn faster than you think and forget faster than you learn, and most study habits fight that instead of working with it.

Two things fix it, and both are boring.

1. Testing beats reviewing. Reading something again feels productive and barely works. Trying to recall it, and failing, is what makes it stick. Every prompt in this course does that on purpose.
2. Spacing beats cramming. The best moment to review something is right when you're about to forget it. Ten minutes a day for a month beats a five-hour weekend by a long way.

blocks.title: Why input matters most
blocks.text: Here's the part most apps won't tell you. Grammar is absorbed, not installed. You pick it up by understanding lots of real Spanish (podcasts, shows, conversation, YouTube), not by drilling rules.

So what is this course for?

These lessons are exposure and awareness. They give you the shape of a thing so that when it goes past you in real speech, you notice it instead of it washing over you.

The lesson makes you aware. The input makes you fluent.

Which means the honest version of the deal:

Everything here is a refresher and a set of examples. The depth comes from you: hours of listening to native speech, and wanting it enough to keep going back.

No app replaces that. This one just makes the hours count for more.

blocks.title: How to use these lessons
blocks.text:
Say every answer out loud before you check. Silent guessing barely works.

Be wrong often. That's how it works, not a failure.

Short and daily beats long and rare.

And go find something to listen to. The rule for picking: you should mostly understand it, and you should actually want to. Bored is worse than easy.

Start where a child starts: simple language, obvious pictures, lots of repetition. That's not beneath you. It's the fastest way in.

Made for learners. The gentlest start, because they slow down and use pictures:

• Dreaming Spanish (YouTube): graded from beginner to advanced, and the most recommended thing there is
• Easy Spanish (YouTube): real street interviews with subtitles in both languages
• Español con Juan: slow, funny, all in Spanish
• Coffee Break Spanish or the Duolingo Spanish Podcast: short, structured, half English at first

Made for children. Simple grammar, repeated constantly, short enough to finish:

• Pocoyó: almost no dialogue, great at the very start
• Peppa Pig and Bluey dubbed in Spanish: short episodes, everyday words
• Plaza Sésamo
• Picture books and graded readers. Olly Richards' Short Stories in Spanish is built for exactly this

Made for everyone else, for when you can follow the gist:

• Something you already know well, dubbed into Spanish. Knowing the plot does the work subtitles would
• Radio Ambulante: real journalism and proper stories, worth hearing for their own sake
• Shows and films from Spain, Mexico and Argentina. The accents differ, and that's worth hearing early
• Music you actually like, with the lyrics up

blocks.title: The only rule that matters
blocks.text:
Pick things you'd choose anyway. If you love cooking, watch Spanish cooking channels. If you love football, watch Spanish football coverage.

Interest is what makes you do the hours, and the hours are what make you fluent.

lessons.title: Two languages, two ways of being
lessons.decision: Why Spanish makes you say things English lets you dodge

blocks.title: Why the difference matters
blocks.text: Spanish isn't English with different words. It makes you say things English lets you leave out. Knowing that up front turns the hard parts into things that make sense, not arbitrary rules.

The easy news first. English and Spanish share a Latin ancestor, and a large slice of English vocabulary came in from that side of the family.

You already own thousands of Spanish words. Much of this course is claiming them, not learning them.

Now the real difference. English has one word for to be. Spanish has two, and makes you pick every time.

Ser is what something is: concrete, settled.
Estar is how it's doing: changeable.

It matters:

Estoy aburrido: I'm bored.
Soy aburrido: I'm boring.

Same English words, one choice apart.

Spanish won't let you blur what you're feeling with what you are.

Another:

Estoy listo: I'm ready.
Soy listo: I'm clever.

Every time you describe yourself in Spanish you answer a question English never asks: is this me, or is this just today?

blocks.title: Why it becomes part of you
blocks.text:
This is a habit of mind, not faster translating.

The grammar becomes part of how you think, because it's how you're able to express yourself. A Spanish speaker has spent their whole life separating essence from state, because the grammar demanded it. That's what you're picking up.

The same split happens with English for, which Spanish divides into por and para.

Gracias por la ayuda: thanks for the help. This is por, the reason or cause, the thing that already happened.

Es para ti: it's for you. This is para, the destination or purpose, where it's headed.

And gender. El and la aren't claims about male and female. They're noun classes, like folders.

The everyday rule is simple:
-o takes el. -a takes la.

El teléfono. La música. That'll be right most of the time.

Now watch it break.

El problema is masculine, despite the -a. Words ending -ma are usually masculine, because they came from Greek and kept their own rules.

La mano is feminine, despite the -o. It comes from Latin manus, which was already feminine, and Spanish kept it that way.

So don't hunt for meaning in gender. Learn the pattern, learn the handful that break it, and past that, native speakers go on what sounds right, because they've heard it ten thousand times.

That's another thing only listening gives you.

blocks.title: Why a second language gives you more
blocks.text:
A second language isn't a worse copy of your first. It hands you moves yours doesn't have.

Spanish lets you say se me cayó, it fell from me, where English makes you say I dropped it. One language assigns blame. The other describes what happened.

Sometimes a true thing is easier to say in your second language than your first.

blocks.title: How to keep going with an AI
blocks.text:
At the end of every lesson there's a button: Keep practising with an AI. It copies a prompt you paste into ChatGPT, Claude, Gemini or any AI chat. The home screen has one too, covering everything you've finished.

The prompt sends the AI to this site to read the course itself, and tells it which lesson you just did and every rule you've learned so far. It asks for sentences that use only those rules, and words from Bedrock's core list: the 4,000 most common words in Spanish.

You won't know most of those words yet, and that's on purpose. When one comes up that you don't know, guess. Say what you think it means, and try the sentence anyway. The AI tells you if you were right and explains it. A wrong guess sticks far better than being told, the same way your mistakes in these lessons do.

Two more things. AIs make mistakes, so if one disagrees with a lesson, trust the lesson and ask it to explain. And Bedrock never sees that conversation. It happens in your AI app, not here.

blocks.title: What comes next
blocks.text:
Everything from here is examples, not the whole picture. Each lesson opens with why the thing matters, then shows you its shape.

The depth comes from your own listening. These lessons just make sure you recognise it when it goes past.

unlocks: the idea of ser (what something is) against estar (how or where it is), not yet used in sentences
gender as a filing system: -o usually takes el, -a usually takes la, with exceptions like el problema and la mano
lessons.ai: This lesson was ideas, not sentences. Ask me questions in English to check I understood them: ser against estar, por against para, and gender as a filing system. Give me English situations ("I'm tired today", "she's a doctor") and ask which kind of to be Spanish would use, and why. Don't ask me to write Spanish sentences yet.

lessons.title: Words you already own

blocks.title: Why free words matter
blocks.text: Most courses start you on phrases you can't take apart. This one starts you on a rule that hands you thousands of words at once. They're ordinary words to a Spanish speaker, so using them makes you sound normal, not textbook.
Nation becomes nación in Spanish. The ending shifts. The word doesn't.

blocks.prompt: Say each one in Spanish out loud, then check all five.

blocks.text: You didn't learn five new words. You learned one rule and collected five. There are thousands more with that same rule.

unlocks: -tion → -ción: English -tion words have a Spanish twin ending in -ción
lessons.ai: Give me English words ending in -tion, one at a time, and I'll say the Spanish. Include one or two where the rule doesn't quite hold and explain those briefly. Remind me that every -ción word is stressed on the last syllable.

lessons.title: Where the emphasis goes
lessons.decision: The accent tells you which syllable to hit

blocks.title: Why emphasis matters
blocks.text: English swallows the syllables it doesn't stress. Spanish doesn't. Every syllable gets its full value, and exactly one gets the emphasis.
Put the emphasis in the wrong place and you often aren't just accented. You're saying a different word.

One more thing before you try it. Spanish vowels are short and pure.

The letter a says ah, not ay. e says eh. i says ee. o says oh. u says oo.

Five sounds, always the same. English has around twenty and changes them constantly.

Now say this out loud before I tell you anything. Commit to a guess.

Getting it wrong right now is the point. The miss is what makes the right answer stick later. A correct guess teaches you far less.

blocks.a: The accent is an instruction: stress the last syllable. And notice the vowels went short: oh, eh, ah, ee, oh. No say, no shun.
Same instruction, same trap. Every vowel is short and clean, and the accent tells you where the weight lands.

blocks.text: Now one with no accent mark, so the rule has to carry you.

blocks.a:
Words ending in a vowel, -n or -s take the emphasis on the second-to-last syllable, with no mark needed.

And that final e gets pronounced. English drops endings. Spanish never does.
This ends in -d, so the default flips: anything ending in a consonant other than -n or -s takes the emphasis on the last syllable.

blocks.text:
That's the whole system.

Ends in a vowel, -n or -s → second-to-last syllable.
Ends in any other consonant → last syllable.
An accent mark → overrides both, always.

Spanish never leaves you guessing where the emphasis goes.

unlocks: Spanish vowels are short and pure: a ah, e eh, i ee, o oh, u oo
stress: ends in a vowel, -n or -s → second-to-last syllable; any other consonant → last syllable; an accent mark overrides both
lessons.ai: Give me Spanish words one at a time (I'm not expected to know what they mean) and ask which syllable takes the stress, and why, using the three rules. Mix words with and without accent marks.

lessons.title: All of them are "la"

blocks.title: Why gender matters
blocks.text: Gender isn't a claim about the world. La mesa doesn't mean tables are womanly. It's a filing system, and its real job is agreement: article, noun and describing word all echo each other. That echo is a lot of why Spanish sounds the way it does.
Every word ending in -ción takes la. Nothing to memorise, because the ending already told you.
One rule just handed you the gender of a few thousand nouns. That's the pattern for this whole course: find the rule, skip the list.

unlocks: -ción words are feminine and take la
lessons.ai: Give me English nouns ending in -tion and ask for the Spanish with its article. Now and then ask me why it's la.

lessons.title: Four more rules

blocks.title: Why patterns matter
blocks.text: You're not collecting words. You're building a converter. Once these are in, most English abstract nouns and adjectives have a Spanish twin you can make on the spot instead of trying to remember it.
-ty becomes -dad, and those are feminine too.
-ous becomes -oso. These describe things.
-ive becomes -ivo, and -ly becomes -mente.
Things, and words to describe them. Next comes what joins the two, and it's the choice from lesson 0.

unlocks: -ty → -dad (also feminine)
-ous → -oso
-ive → -ivo
-ly → -mente
describing words agree: -o with el words, -a with la words
lessons.ai: Give me English words ending in -ty, -ous, -ive and -ly, mixed up, and I'll convert them. For -dad words, ask for the article too. Point out any word where the rule breaks.

lessons.title: Ser — what something is

blocks.title: Why ser matters
blocks.text: This is the identity verb, and it's concrete. Reaching for ser says something is that way by nature. Describe yourself with it and you're saying this is who I am, so it carries more weight than English am does.

First, something I've been dodging. I keep saying ser, then writing es. They look like different words. They aren't.

Spanish verbs have a base form, the one in the dictionary, and then they change shape depending on who's doing it. That's called conjugation.

Ser is the base form: to be. You'd never say it on its own. Its shapes:

soy: I am
eres: you are
es: he, she or it is
somos: we are
son: they are

So es is ser wearing its he/she/it clothes.

English does this too. You've just stopped noticing: be becomes am, is, are, was, were. Spanish is only more consistent about it.

For now you need one shape: es.
Es: is. For what something is at heart: identity, origin, what kind of thing it is.
Notice famosa, not famoso. It's la universidad, so the describing word follows it to -a. That's the agreement from lesson 3 doing its job.
One word, and every noun and adjective you've collected just became a sentence.

unlocks: es (from ser): what something is, its identity or kind
lessons.ai: Give me English sentences shaped like 'the [noun] is [describing word]' using my words. Check that the describing word agrees (famosa with la universidad).

lessons.title: Estar — how something is

blocks.title: Why estar matters
blocks.text: Estar is the verb of right now, and it bends. It's how Spanish speakers talk about mood, condition and place, things that could be different tomorrow. Learning to reach for it is learning to stop turning passing states into permanent claims about yourself.
Está also means is. But it's for where something is, or how it's doing at the moment.
Both words are is. English uses one word for two jobs and never makes you notice. Spanish splits them, and the next lesson is that split.

unlocks: está (from estar): where something is, or how it's doing right now
aquí (here) and allí (there)
lessons.ai: Give me sentences about where things are, or the state they're in right now, using está.

lessons.title: Ser or estar

blocks.title: Why the choice matters
blocks.text: This is the mistake English speakers make most, and it changes what you're saying. Say soy aburrido when you meant estoy aburrido and you've announced you're boring, not bored. The grammar makes a claim about you either way.
The working rule, and it's a good one: permanent → ser, temporary → estar. That carries you through most of what you say day to day, so lean on it.

Clearest side by side:

El hielo es frío: ice is cold. That's what ice is.
La sopa está fría: the soup is cold. It isn't supposed to be.

Same adjective. One is the nature of the thing, one is its current state.

Now the seam, so it doesn't blindside you later.

Es joven — he is young. Being young is about as temporary as things get, and it still takes ser.

Why? Because it's a category he belongs to, not a condition he's in.

So permanent or temporary is the surface of something deeper: am I naming what it is, or how it's doing or where it is?

Essence or category → ser.
Condition or place → estar.

Use permanent or temporary as your everyday guide. When it feels wrong, drop to this one.

blocks.en: the conversation is important — essence or condition?
the conversation is here — which one?

blocks.title: Why this becomes a habit
blocks.text:
Every time you use one of these you make a small statement about what's essential and what's passing. That's the habit of mind, and it's the biggest single thing Spanish changes about how you describe yourself.

You'll hear this hundreds of times in real speech. Now you'll notice it.

unlocks: choosing es or está: essence or category → ser; condition or place → estar
lessons.ai: Make me choose between es and está every time. Mix essence and category sentences with location and condition ones. When I get one wrong, first ask me 'is that what it is, or how or where it is?' before telling me.

lessons.title: Verbs you already own

blocks.title: Why the base form matters
blocks.text: English needs two words for to prepare. Spanish folds the to into the ending. That's why the next six lessons work: the base form never changes, so once you can put something in front of it, every verb you recognise comes along.
Preparar is to prepare. The -ar does the job of the word to.
You can only recognise these so far. From the next lesson on, you'll be using every one of them.

unlocks: base-form verbs end in -ar, -er or -ir, and they don't change after an opening
lessons.ai: Give me English verbs and ask for the Spanish base form. Stick to verbs with obvious Spanish twins (organise, decide, permit, visit, prepare, accept, celebrate, present, consider, invite, use, control).

lessons.title: Tener que — having to

blocks.title: Why tener que matters
blocks.text: Spanish tends to have states where English is them. Tengo hambre is I have hunger, not I am hungry. Obligation works the same way: you don't become obliged, you carry an obligation.
Tengo que: I have to. What comes after it doesn't change at all.

blocks.en: I have to visit the university

blocks.text: Learn this shape properly. Five more openings use it.

unlocks: tengo que + base form: I have to
lessons.ai: Give me 'I have to ...' sentences using tengo que, a base-form verb and my nouns.

lessons.title: Deber — ought to

blocks.title: Why deber matters
blocks.text: Tengo que is pressure from outside: circumstances say so. Debo is pressure from inside, closer to duty or conscience. Spanish separates the two, and English blurs both into have to and should.
Debo: I should. Same shape you just learned.
Second opening, nothing new to learn. That's what the shape buys you.

unlocks: debo + base form: I should
lessons.ai: Mix 'I have to' (tengo que) and 'I should' (debo). Sometimes describe a situation and ask which fits: pressure from outside, or duty from inside.

lessons.title: Poder — being able, and saying no
lessons.decision: puedo + base form, no in front, then ser and estar after any opening

blocks.title: Why no matters
blocks.text: Negation is where Spanish is simpler, so enjoy it. English rebuilds the sentence: I decide becomes I don't decide, with a helper verb out of nowhere. Spanish puts no at the front and leaves everything else alone.
Puedo: I can.
Now negate anything. No goes in front. Nothing else moves.

blocks.en: I don't have to visit the university
blocks.es: no tengo que visitar la universidad
blocks.p: noh TEN-goh keh vee-see-TAHR lah oo-nee-vehr-see-DAHD

blocks.text: One small word, and everything you've built so far just doubled.

One more thing has been hiding in plain sight. Ser and estar are base forms too. Es and está are just those two with the ending changed, so they go after an opening like any other verb.

Which means the old choice comes back. Before you answer, decide: is it what something is, or where and how it is right now?

unlocks: puedo + base form: I can
no goes in front of the verb, and nothing else moves
ser and estar can follow any opening as base forms
lessons.ai: Practise puedo and negation with no, mixed with tengo que and debo. Include sentences where ser or estar follow an opening (tengo que estar aquí), so I still have to choose between them.

lessons.title: Querer — wanting

blocks.title: Why querer matters
blocks.text: Querer is also how you tell someone you love them: te quiero. English has one word for love and makes it enormous. Spanish has a warm everyday one and a weightier one (te amo), and knowing which to use is something you'll only get from listening.
Quiero: I want.

blocks.en: I want to visit the university
I want to prepare the presentation

blocks.text: Fourth opening. Still the same shape.

unlocks: quiero + base form: I want to
lessons.ai: Mix quiero with the earlier openings and with no. Every few sentences, put ser or estar after the opening.

lessons.title: Necesitar — needing

blocks.title: Why necesitar matters
blocks.text: This one tests whether the converter from lesson 4 is running yet. You've never been taught this word, and you should still see it coming.
Necesito: I need. Look at it: necessitate. You could almost have guessed it, and soon you'll guess right often enough to stop noticing.

blocks.en: I need to organise the education

unlocks: necesito + base form: I need to
lessons.ai: Mix necesito with all the earlier openings. Include a few verbs I haven't been taught that are obvious English twins, and see if I can guess them.

lessons.title: Ir a — going to
lessons.decision: voy a + base form, then all six openings mixed

blocks.title: Why voy a matters
blocks.text: Spanish has a real future tense, and in everyday speech people mostly don't use it. Voy a is what you'll actually hear. It isn't a beginner's shortcut you'll replace later. It's what native speakers say.
Voy a: I'm going to. Two words, and they behave like the rest.

blocks.en: I'm going to visit the university
I'm not going to accept the situation
blocks.es: no voy a aceptar la situación
blocks.p: noh voy ah ah-sep-TAHR lah see-twah-see-OHN

blocks.text: Now all of it at once. Every sentence below needs two decisions: which opening, and whether ser or estar comes after it. Take your time on each one. Slow and right beats fast and guessed.

blocks.en: I'm not going to be here

blocks.text: Six openings (tengo que, debo, puedo, quiero, necesito, voy a) across every verb you recognise, with no on any of them. Add ser and estar and you can describe things, place them, and say what you mean to do about them.

blocks.title: Why the listening comes next
blocks.text:
Every one of those sentences made you choose what's essential and what's passing. That choice is what you're actually learning.

Now go and hear it. Put on something in Spanish and catch ser, estar and these six openings going past. You'll hear them within minutes, and that's where this starts turning into fluency.

unlocks: voy a + base form: I'm going to
lessons.ai: Mix all six openings (tengo que, debo, puedo, quiero, necesito, voy a), with and without no, and with ser or estar after them. Each sentence should make me choose twice: which opening, and which to be.

lessons.title: Gustar — what pleases you
lessons.decision: me gusta + a thing or a base form

blocks.title: Why gustar matters
blocks.text: English puts you in charge: I like it. Spanish turns it around. The thing does the pleasing, and you're on the receiving end. Me gusta is it pleases me. See it that way and the odd word order stops being odd.
Me gusta: it pleases me. That's how you say I like. The thing you like goes after it, because it's the one doing the work.
It takes a base-form verb too, just like the six openings. Me gusta decidir: deciding pleases me.
No goes in front of the whole thing: no me gusta.

The easy mistake is yo gusto. That says I am pleasing, which isn't what you meant. Keep the person as me, the receiver.

Me is to me. It's the same little word as in se me cayó from lesson 0. Spanish likes putting the person on the receiving end.
One thing to file away. When more than one thing does the pleasing, it's gustan: me gustan. You'll hear it constantly, and now you'll know why it changed.

unlocks: me gusta + a thing or a base form: I like (it pleases me)
no me gusta
plural things take gustan (only met, not practised)
lessons.ai: Practise me gusta and no me gusta with my nouns and base-form verbs. Watch for 'yo gusto' or 'me gusto' and explain the it-pleases-me logic when I slip. Keep to singular things; don't make me use gustan yet.

lessons.title: Estoy + -ando — happening right now

blocks.title: Why the -ing form matters
blocks.text: English uses -ing for everything: I'm working, I'm working tomorrow, working is hard. Spanish mostly keeps its -ing for one job: what's in progress at this moment. So it's easier than English, and you'll hear it less than you'd expect.
First, estoy: I am, in the estar sense. You know está. This is its I shape.

Now the -ing. Drop the ending and add -ando for -ar verbs, -iendo for -er and -ir.

Preparar → preparando.
Decidir → decidiendo.
Why estar and never ser? Because something in progress is a state you're in right now. It's lesson 7's choice again, and here it always lands on estar.
The trap: English says I'm visiting the university tomorrow. Spanish won't use estoy for a plan. Plans go with voy a: voy a visitar la universidad mañana (mañana: tomorrow).

vocab.en: I am (how or where I am)

unlocks: estoy: I am, in the estar sense
-ando (for -ar) and -iendo (for -er, -ir): the -ing form
estoy + -ando/-iendo only for what's in progress right now; plans use voy a
lessons.ai: Make me choose: is this happening right now (estoy + -ando/-iendo), or is it a plan (voy a + base form)? Include English -ing sentences that should NOT become estoy + -ando in Spanish, and see if I catch them.

lessons.title: Preparo — saying you do it

blocks.title: Why the -o matters
blocks.text: Six lessons let you talk about doing things without ever changing the verb: an opening did the work. Now the other way, saying plainly that you do something. It's one ending, and almost every verb takes it.

Drop -ar, -er or -ir and add -o. Preparar → preparo: I prepare.

That -o already means I, so Spanish doesn't need yo in front. Add yo only when you want to stress it: I prepare it, not you.
Where does the weight go? Preparo: pre-PA-ro. It ends in a vowel, so the second-to-last syllable, as lesson 2 said. Hold on to that. A past tense later depends on moving it.

Now look back at your openings. Debo and necesito are this exact rule. Quiero and puedo are the same -o on a stem that shifts (querer → quier-, poder → pued-). Tengo and voy just break it. The most common verbs usually do.

blocks.en: I want to visit the university, and I visit it
blocks.es: quiero visitar la universidad y la visito
blocks.p: kee-EH-roh vee-see-TAHR lah oo-nee-vehr-see-DAHD ee lah vee-SEE-toh

blocks.text: That last one was a preview: y is and, and la visito is I visit it. The next lesson is that la.

unlocks: any regular verb, I form: drop -ar/-er/-ir, add -o (preparo, decido)
the -o already means I, so yo is only for stress
stress on preparo falls on the second-to-last syllable
y: and
lessons.ai: Give me 'I + verb' sentences. Mix the plain form (preparo) with openings (quiero preparar), so I have to notice when the verb changes and when it stays a base form. Check my stress: preparo is stressed on PA.

lessons.title: Lo and la — it
lessons.decision: lo or la for 'it', in front of the verb

blocks.title: Why lo and la matter
blocks.text: Spanish doesn't like repeating a noun it already has. Once the presentation has come up, it becomes la. And you already know that word.
La is the, and it's also it for a feminine thing. Lo is it for a masculine thing. Same filing system as lesson 3.
The new part is where it goes: in front of the verb. La preparo: it I-prepare. English says I prepare it. Spanish puts the it first.
With no, the order is no, then it, then the verb. El problema from lesson 0 is masculine, so it becomes lo.
With an opening, it can go on the end of the base form instead: quiero prepararla. Or in front of the opening: la quiero preparar. Both are normal, and they mean the same.

blocks.en: I want to prepare it (the presentation)
I have to decide it (the problem)
blocks.es: tengo que decidirlo · lo tengo que decidir

unlocks: lo / la = it (masculine / feminine), in front of a conjugated verb
no + lo/la + verb
with an opening, lo/la can attach to the base form (prepararla) or go in front (la quiero preparar)
lessons.ai: Give me a sentence with a noun, then a follow-up where I replace the noun with lo or la. Check gender and where I put it, including with no and with openings.

lessons.title: Tú — talking to you

blocks.title: Why tú matters
blocks.text: Until now you've only talked about yourself. To talk to someone, the verb changes again, and Spanish gives you a choice English lost centuries ago: a familiar you and a polite one. This lesson is the familiar one, tú. The polite one is next.

For tú, drop the ending and add -as for -ar verbs, -es for -er and -ir.

Preparas: you prepare.
Decides: you decide.
The openings do it too, with the same quirks as before: tienes que, debes, puedes, quieres, necesitas, vas a. And estás, and eres from lesson 5.
A question is the same sentence with your voice going up at the end. No do, no swapping words around. Written Spanish marks it at both ends: ¿puedes decidir?

blocks.en: Do you want to visit the university?
You don't have to accept it (the situation)

unlocks: tú (familiar you): -as for -ar verbs, -es for -er and -ir
tú forms of the openings: tienes que, debes, puedes, quieres, necesitas, vas a
estás and eres
questions keep the same word order, with rising voice and ¿ ?
lessons.ai: Talk to me as tú. Give me sentences addressed to a friend, and questions to ask them. Mix statements and questions so I practise both the -as/-es endings and the rising-voice questions.

lessons.title: Él, ella, usted — one form, three people

blocks.title: Why this form matters
blocks.text: Here's a gift. The form for he and she is also the polite you. Usted started life as vuestra merced, 'your grace', and you talk to a grace the way you talk about someone. So one form covers three people.

Take the tú form and drop the -s.

Preparas → prepara.
Decides → decide.

You've already met three of these without knowing: es, está and gusta.
With usted you use the same form, and you say usted when it isn't obvious who you mean.

blocks.en: Do you want to visit the university? (polite)
She has to accept it (the situation)

blocks.text: Which you? Tú for friends, family, children and people your age. Usted for strangers older than you, officials, and anyone you'd call sir or ma'am. It shifts by country, so listen to what people around you use. When in doubt, start with usted. People will tell you to switch.

unlocks: él / ella / usted share one form: the tú form without its -s (prepara, decide)
usted is the polite you; tú for friends, family, children, people your age
puede, quiere, tiene que, debe, necesita, va a
lessons.ai: Mix sentences about a he or she with polite questions to usted. Sometimes describe who I'm talking to (a friend, a shop owner, a grandmother) and ask me to pick tú or usted.

lessons.title: He decidido — the perfect

blocks.title: Why the perfect comes first
blocks.text: English already gave you this one. I have decided is he decidido: have plus a past form, in the same order. It's the easiest past Spanish has, so it comes first.

He is I have, but only for this job. Owning something is still tengo.

Then the verb with -ado for -ar and -ido for -er and -ir.
Preparar → preparado. Decidir → decidido.
For other people it's has (you) and ha (he, she, usted). Same pattern as lesson 20: drop the tú form's -s.
With it, lo or la goes in front of he: la he preparado. The he and the -ado never split up.

unlocks: he / has / ha + -ado (for -ar) or -ido (for -er, -ir): have done
lo/la go in front of he, has, ha
he and the -ado/-ido form never split
lessons.ai: Give me 'have done' sentences for I, you and he/she, with and without no, and with lo or la. Mix in an earlier opening now and then so I don't go on autopilot.

lessons.title: Commands — telling a friend
lessons.decision: the tú command is the he/she form

blocks.title: Why commands matter
blocks.text: Telling someone to do something is half of everyday speech: wait, look, pass it. Spanish makes the friendly command almost free, because you already know the form.

The tú command is the same shape as he/she.

¡Prepara! Prepare!
¡Decide! Decide!

No you, no helper word.

With it, the lo or la goes on the end, and a written accent appears to keep the weight where it was. Prepara + la → ¡prepárala! The stress didn't move. Lesson 2's rules just need the mark to say so now.

blocks.en: Prepare it! (the presentation, to a friend)
Accept it! (the situation, to a friend)

blocks.text: Two things wait until later. Polite commands to usted and don't commands both flip the vowel (¡prepare!, ¡no prepares!). That flip is the subjunctive, and it has its own lesson near the end. Until then, no tienes que (you don't have to) is a friendly way round it.

unlocks: the tú command is the he/she form: ¡prepara!, ¡decide!
lo/la attach to the end of a command, with a written accent: ¡prepárala!
lessons.ai: Give me situations where I'd tell a friend to do something, and I'll say the command. Include some with it (lo/la) attached so I have to add the accent mark. Don't ask for negative or polite commands yet.

lessons.title: Preparé — it happened
lessons.decision: -é / -í for I, -ó / -ió for he and she

blocks.title: Why the preterite matters
blocks.text: This is the past for things that happened and finished: I decided, she visited. It's the tense stories run on, and it hinges on the stress rules from lesson 2.

For I: drop the ending, add -é for -ar verbs and -í for -er and -ir.

Preparé: I prepared.
Decidí: I decided.

The accent is part of the word.
For he, she and usted: -ó and -ió. Preparó: she prepared. Decidió: he decided. For tú: -aste and -iste. Preparaste, decidiste.

blocks.a: Preparo is I prepare, weight on PA. Preparó is she prepared, weight on the end. Same letters, different person, different time. Put the weight in the wrong place and you've said something else.

blocks.text: The common verbs break the pattern, as usual: fui (I went, and also I was), tuve (I had), pude (I managed to). You'll pick them up by hearing them.

unlocks: preterite: I -é / -í; you -aste / -iste; he, she, usted -ó / -ió
stress separates preparo (I prepare) from preparó (she prepared)
fui, tuve, pude (common irregulars, met)
lessons.ai: Give me finished past events for I, you and he/she. Mix in present sentences (preparo) so I have to hear the difference between preparo and preparó, and check my stress.

lessons.title: Preparaba — how things were
lessons.decision: -aba / -ía for the scene, not the event

blocks.title: Why a second past matters
blocks.text: The preterite is a camera click: it happened. Spanish has a second past for everything around the click: what was going on, what used to happen, how things were. English blurs that into was -ing and used to.

Drop the ending and add -aba for -ar verbs, -ía for -er and -ir. The same form works for I and for he and she.

Preparaba: I was preparing, I used to prepare.

blocks.en: I used to visit the university

blocks.text: The two scene-setters you'll hear most are era (from ser) and estaba (from estar). They keep their split in the past: what it was against how or where it was.

unlocks: imperfect: -aba (for -ar), -ía (for -er, -ir), same for I and he/she
era (ser) and estaba (estar) keep the ser/estar split in the past
lessons.ai: Give me sentences about how things used to be or what was going on, for I and he/she. Include era and estaba so I still have to choose between ser and estar.

lessons.title: Preterite or imperfect
lessons.decision: the event, or the scene around it

blocks.title: Why this choice matters
blocks.text: This is the second big choice, after ser and estar, and it works the same way. Spanish makes you decide something English leaves vague: was this an event, or the background to one?

Think of a film. The imperfect is the scene: what was going on, how things were. The preterite is what happens in it, the moment someone acts.

Preparaba la presentación cuando decidí. I was preparing the presentation when I decided. (cuando: when)
Two questions settle most cases. Did it start and finish? Preterite. Was it ongoing, repeated or describing? Imperfect.

blocks.en: I was visiting the university when I decided
The information was here when I visited
blocks.es: la información estaba aquí cuando visité
blocks.p: lah een-for-mah-see-OHN ehs-TAH-bah ah-KEE KWAHN-doh vee-see-TEH

blocks.en: I prepared the presentation and accepted the situation
blocks.es: preparé la presentación y acepté la situación
blocks.p: preh-pah-REH lah preh-sen-tah-see-OHN ee ah-sep-TEH lah see-twah-see-OHN

blocks.text: Sometimes the choice changes the meaning. Quería is I wanted, the state. Quise is I tried, the moment. No quise is I refused.

blocks.title: Why the ear gets there first
blocks.text: As with ser and estar, you'll get this right by ear long before you get it right by rule. Listen to anyone telling a story and you'll hear the scene in -aba and -ía, and the events in -é and -ó.

unlocks: preterite for events that started and finished; imperfect for the scene, the ongoing and the repeated
cuando: when
quería (I wanted) against quise (I tried) and no quise (I refused)
lessons.ai: Give me short two-part stories in English where one part is the scene and one is the event, and I'll put them in Spanish. When I pick the wrong past, ask me 'event or scene?' before correcting me.

lessons.title: Saber or conocer

blocks.title: Why the split matters
blocks.text: Another English verb doing two jobs. Know covers knowing a fact and knowing a person or a place. Spanish splits them, and the split is easy once you see it.

Sé: I know a fact, or how to do something.
Conozco: I know a person or a place. I'm familiar with it.
Sé plus a base form means I know how to. Sé organizar: I know how to organise. No word for how needed.

blocks.en: I know how to organise the information
Do you know how to prepare the presentation?

blocks.text: Sé carries an accent so it isn't mixed up with se without one. That one's next.

unlocks: sé / sabes: facts and how-to (sé + base form = I know how to)
conozco / conoces: people and places
lessons.ai: Make me choose between sé/sabes and conozco/conoces every time. Mix facts, skills, people and places. When I get one wrong, ask 'a fact or a familiarity?' first.

lessons.title: Se — when nobody in particular does it

blocks.title: Why se matters
blocks.text: English needs a stand-in subject: one says, they say, people say, or a passive like it is said. Spanish uses one small word, se, and you'll see it on signs everywhere: se habla español, Spanish spoken here. (hablar: to speak)

Se plus the he/she form means it gets done, by nobody in particular.

Se prepara: it's prepared, one prepares it.
¿Se puede? Can one? It's also how you ask may I come in?

blocks.en: You can visit the university here (one can)
blocks.es: aquí se puede visitar la universidad
blocks.p: ah-KEE seh PWEH-deh vee-see-TAHR lah oo-nee-vehr-see-DAHD

blocks.text: Remember se me cayó from lesson 0? It's a close cousin of this se. The thing fell, me says who it happened to, and nobody is to blame. That's exactly why Spanish speakers reach for it.

unlocks: se + he/she form: one does it, it gets done (se habla, se puede)
¿se puede? as 'may I?'
lessons.ai: Give me English sentences with 'one', 'people', 'they' or a passive ('it is prepared'), and I'll turn them into se sentences. Mix in a few that need a real person instead, so I don't use se for everything.

lessons.title: Prepararía — would

blocks.title: Why would matters
blocks.text: Would softens everything. It's how you ask nicely and how you imagine. Spanish builds it the easy way: you don't even drop the ending.

Keep the whole base form and add -ía.

Preparar → prepararía: I would prepare.
Decidir → decidiría: I would decide.

Same ending for every verb type.
Three verbs you know get a polite version. Debería: I ought to, softer than debo. Podría: I could (poder shortens to podr-). Me gustaría: I'd like, the polite way to ask for anything.

blocks.en: I ought to prepare the presentation
I'd like to visit the university

unlocks: conditional: the whole base form + -ía (prepararía, decidiría)
debería (I ought to), podría (I could), me gustaría (I'd like)
lessons.ai: Practise would-sentences, and polite requests with me gustaría, podría and debería. Sometimes give me a blunt sentence (quiero visitar) and ask me to make it polite.

lessons.title: Quiero que decidas — wanting someone else to

blocks.title: Why the subjunctive matters
blocks.text: This is the part people dread, and the core is one idea. When you want, need or hope that someone else does something, Spanish marks that action as not real yet. It does it by flipping a vowel.

Compare:

Quiero preparar: I want to prepare. Same person, so a base form.
Quiero que prepares: I want you to prepare. A different person, so que plus a new form.
The new form swaps the vowel. -ar verbs take e: preparas → prepares. -er and -ir verbs take a: decides → decidas. It's the opposite vowel, which is why it sounds wrong at first.

blocks.en: I need you to prepare the presentation

blocks.text: It also follows a judgement about something: es importante que, es posible que, me gusta que.

blocks.en: It's important that you visit the university
blocks.es: es importante que visites la universidad
blocks.p: ess eem-pohr-TAHN-teh keh vee-SEE-tehs lah oo-nee-vehr-see-DAHD

blocks.text: This is the flip lesson 22 promised. Don't commands use it: ¡no prepares! So do polite commands to usted: ¡prepare!

unlocks: present subjunctive: the opposite vowel (-ar verbs → e, -er/-ir verbs → a)
after quiero que, necesito que, es importante que, es posible que
negative tú commands (¡no prepares!) and usted commands (¡prepare!)
lessons.ai: Give me sentences where I want, need or judge something someone else does, mixed with sentences where I do it myself (quiero preparar). I have to notice when it needs que + the flipped vowel and when it doesn't.

lessons.title: Si pudiera — if I could

blocks.title: Why this last piece matters
blocks.text: The last piece is for things that aren't true: if I had more time, if I were you. English barely marks it. Spanish pairs a special past with the would form from lesson 28.

Drop the ending and add -ara for -ar verbs, -iera for -er and -ir: preparara, decidiera.

It's built from the preterite, so the irregulars carry over: fuera (from fui), pudiera (from pude), tuviera (from tuve).

The pattern: si + this form, then the -ía form.

Si decidiera, prepararía la presentación. If I decided, I'd prepare the presentation. (si: if)

blocks.en: If I visited the university, I would decide
If I could, I would visit the university
If the conversation were important, I would accept it
blocks.es: si la conversación fuera importante, la aceptaría
blocks.p: see lah kohn-vehr-sah-see-OHN FWEH-rah eem-pohr-TAHN-teh lah ah-sep-tah-REE-ah

blocks.text: It's also the past of lesson 29. Quiero que decidas becomes quería que decidieras: I wanted you to decide.

blocks.en: I wanted you to prepare the presentation

blocks.title: Where this leaves you
blocks.text:
That's the map. Every structure Spanish uses most is now something you've met. The course can't make them automatic. Only hours of listening do that.

What it can do is make sure that when you hear si pudiera in a song or a show, you know exactly what's going on. Keep listening, and keep using the AI button to practise whatever still feels slow.

unlocks: past subjunctive: -ara (for -ar), -iera (for -er, -ir), built from the preterite (fuera, pudiera, tuviera)
si + past subjunctive, then the -ía form
quería que + past subjunctive
lessons.ai: Give me 'if' sentences about things that aren't true, and wishes about what someone else did. Mix in real conditions (if it rains, I stay) so I have to notice which ones need the -ara/-iera form.
